rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their angel mythology assumes they are God's beloved daughters whose intercession secures worldly favors and future aid, revealing their denial of the Hereafter as the day each deed receives justice.
rows.anchor: It is these people who have named angels after women and concocted the mythology that they are beloved daughters of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their folk tale evades accountability through conjecture and fancy; conjecture cannot replace reality, and its falsity will become clear when reality appears.
rows.anchor: Merely to fulfil their fancies, they are indulging in blatant conjecture.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zann contrasts with guidance, knowledge, and truth: knowledge may come through innate guidance, intellect, or revelation, while claims supported by none of these are baseless speculation.
rows.anchor: What is not substantiated by innate guidance and intellect nor by divine revelation is in fact totally speculative and baseless.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs knew that a claim unsupported by reason cannot count as knowledge and is only conjecture without a basis.
rows.anchor: The Arabs were fully aware of this reality that what is not substantiated by reason cannot be regarded as knowledge; it is mere conjecture

rows.speaker: Ṭarfah ibn al-‘Abd
rows.claim: Ṭarfah's cited line distinguishes knowledge-based knowing from conjecture.
rows.anchor: The famous classical poet Ṭarfah ibn al-‘Abd has distinguished between conjecture and knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says another aspect of conjecture will be explained under 69:20.
rows.anchor: which I will inshā’Allāh explain under the following verse of Sūrah al-Ḥāqqah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not pursue people who arrogantly prefer their own fancies, conjecture, and evil over God's guidance, knowledge, and good; after conveying the message, he has discharged his duty and they will soon face the consequences.
rows.anchor: instead of following the guidance of God they want to follow their own fancies and instead of knowledge want to rely on conjecture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr here refers to the Qur'an, which reminds them of the Hereafter and its responsibilities that they neglect because they rely on imaginary deities.
rows.anchor: refers to the Qur’ ān. It is used for it at many instances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their denial stems from treating this life and its attractions as their real objective.
rows.anchor: refer to the real reason behind their denial: they have regarded this life and its lures to be their real objective.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They attend only to the world's outward form and neither perceive nor desire its deeper reality, though that reality should be their priority; the universe's evident Creator makes a merely playful purpose implausible.
rows.anchor: neither do they have access to the reality behind this external form nor do they have any desire for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's phrasing exposes their narrow-mindedness: temporary pleasures distract them from reality, while timidity and deprivation keep them from pursuing the eternal kingdom to which the Qur'an calls them.
rows.anchor: that it is merely their narrow mindedness and meanness that they are lured by its external form and have become indifferent to its reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites 30:7 to explain this contrast between knowing worldly appearances and neglecting the life to come.
rows.anchor: This aspect is explained by the following verse of Sūrah al-Rūm:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing verse reassures the Prophet and warns worldly-minded people: God knows who strays and who is guided, judges each justly, and will neither let the strayed escape nor withhold aid and mercy from those enduring hardship for His cause.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is addressed and told that he should now ignore them; his Lord fully knows those who have deviated from His path as well as those who are rightly guided.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section III (verses 31–53) further explains and emphasizes the preceding section; its opening theme is God's sole control of the heavens and earth, ensuring punishment of sinners and reward for the righteous without divine partners.
rows.anchor: The succeeding verses further explain and emphasize what is stated in the previous section.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming Paradise through intercessors, lineage, or service to the sanctuary will be cast into Hell; those who avoid usurping rights and public indecency may be forgiven for sins if they repent, for God's mercy is vast.
rows.anchor: because of their intercessors or because of their lineage and race or because of some apparent service to the House of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who boast of holiness should remember their earthly origin in mud, sludge, and impure fluid rather than claim to be sacred.
rows.anchor: a creature made from mud, sludge and an impure fluid should not claim to be so holy and sacred.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi wonders at people who boast of Abrahamic or Mosaic association and expect high rank while withholding charity, since those scriptures teach that no one bears another's burden and each faces the fruit of his own deeds.
rows.anchor: the most prominent teaching of Abraham (sws) and Moses (sws) was that in the Hereafter no one will bear the burden of another person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God controls joy and grief, life and death, provision and children, prosperity and poverty, so everyone should turn to Him at all times.
rows.anchor: sorrow and happiness, life and death, subsistence and children, affluence and poverty are all under the control of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who worship Sirius and attribute spring's blessings to it should remember that God is also the Lord of Sirius.
rows.anchor: the blessings of spring are the result of its bestowal should remember that God is the Lord of Sirius as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier nations also went astray like the Quraysh, so the latter should learn from their fate in history.
rows.anchor: previous nations are briefly referred to in that they too were led astray the way the Quraysh were

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh should learn from earlier peoples' recorded fate and avoid provoking God's wrath.
rows.anchor: in history and not invite the wrath of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prior refutation of polytheism and intercession entails that God's sole dominion over heaven and earth leaves no one able to challenge or influence His authority and decisions.
rows.anchor: the dominion of the heavens and the earth is in the hands of God. No one has a share in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In yajzi, the lām marks consequence rather than cause: because God alone rules, He necessarily punishes sinners who rely on self-appointed deities, and no one can rescue them; He richly rewards the pious without requiring anyone's intercession.
rows.anchor: to state the cause but to state the consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's justice means sinners receive no more than the evils they committed, while His graciousness adds favors beyond the righteous' deserved reward.
rows.anchor: the righteous will not be merely rewarded for their virtues; God will bless them further with His favours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An occasional sin by those who avoid grave sins and open indecency is a brief stumble: like people inclined to cleanliness, they do not dwell in it but repent and reform promptly.
rows.anchor: these people too do not live in sin; they try to cleanse themselves as soon as a sin is committed by repenting and reforming themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-lamam and lamam mean to stay briefly at a place.
rows.anchor: mean to stay at a place for a short period.
